brief.entity: Spencer Alexander Lawyers is a Box Hill, Melbourne law firm setting up companies and drafting shareholder agreements and constitutions for founders, family businesses and co-owners, and acting when co-owners fall out, with the principal overseeing every matter.
bullets: A proprietary company needs at least one member and at least one director who ordinarily resides in Australia, and can have no more than 50 shareholders who are not employees.
Every director needs a director identification number, or must have applied for one, before being appointed.

A company's constitution, with any replaceable rules of the Corporations Act that apply to it, is a contract between the company and each member and between the members themselves, and the constitution can be changed by a special resolution passed by at least 75 per cent of the votes cast.
A shareholder agreement binds only those who sign it, so it works alongside the constitution rather than replacing it.

paras: We act for founders starting a company together, families bringing the next generation or an investor into the business, owners whose company was set up years ago with nothing agreed between them, and co-owners who have started to disagree. The best time to agree the rules is before anyone needs them, while everyone is still on good terms.

Many of the disputes that end businesses begin between co-owners who never agreed in writing how decisions are made and how one of them can leave, and our guide to shareholder agreements explains what a good one covers.

items.p: We register a proprietary company with ASIC, with its constitution, consents, register of members, share certificates and first resolutions, and an ABN and GST registration if needed, working alongside your accountant so the legal and tax positions pull in the same direction. The company exists from the start of the day it is registered.

We draft the agreement around what the owners have agreed: which decisions need everyone's consent, how shares can be sold or transferred, what breaks a deadlock, how an owner leaves or is bought out and at what value, any restraints, and how disputes are resolved.

Without a constitution of its own, a company's internal management is generally governed by the Act's replaceable rules. Under them, for example, the directors of a proprietary company can refuse to register a share transfer for any reason, and new shares must be offered first to existing holders of that class in proportion to their holdings unless the members resolve otherwise. We draft the constitution and the agreement to work together.

Where a company's affairs are conducted against the interests of the members as a whole, or in a way that is oppressive, unfairly prejudicial or unfairly discriminatory to a member, the court can make a wide range of orders, including that one owner buy the other's shares or that the company be wound up. We act for owners on either side, and a good agreement sets out a way through a deadlock before it comes to that.

sections.h2: How the two documents work together.
paras: The constitution binds the company and every member, and can be changed by special resolution. A shareholder agreement is a contract, so it binds only those who sign it, and it cannot change the constitution by itself. A well drafted agreement usually provides that it prevails between the shareholders who sign it, and obliges them to change the constitution to remove any conflict.

Equal owners need this most. When two owners each hold half the shares, neither can outvote the other, and decisions that need a majority of the directors or the shareholders can stall entirely, so the agreement should say what happens next, often a process for one owner to buy the other out at a value worked out in an agreed way.

sections.h2: What to have with you when you call.
paras: Whatever you have to hand: if the company already exists, its constitution, an ASIC company extract, any agreement between the owners and the latest financial statements, and if it does not exist yet, the names of the proposed directors and shareholders and how the shares will be held, with your questions. If you have little on paper, that is fine too. The first conversation is about understanding your situation, not testing your paperwork. We can speak by phone or video, or meet at Suite 10, 1 Main Street, Box Hill, a short walk from Box Hill station, with parking at Box Hill Central.

process.h2: How a company is set up.

steps.d: Before we begin, the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorism Financing Act 2006 (Cth) requires us to verify the identity of our client and of the people who will direct, own or control the company. Each director signs a consent to act and needs a director identification number, or an application for one, before being appointed.
We lodge the application, and once ASIC registers the company it exists from the start of that day, with the members, directors and any secretary named in the application.
Each member agrees in writing to the constitution before the application is lodged, so the company adopts it on registration, and the shareholders sign their agreement once its terms are settled.

faqs.q: Do we need a shareholder agreement if the company has a constitution?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. The constitution sets the company's internal rules and binds every member, but it is commonly a standard document that says little about what the owners have agreed between themselves, such as what happens in a deadlock or when one of them wants to leave. A shareholder agreement deals with those questions in detail and binds the shareholders who sign it.

faqs.q: Does a shareholder agreement override the constitution?
faqs.a: Not by itself. As a contract, it binds only those who sign it, and it cannot change the constitution, which needs a special resolution passed by at least 75 per cent of the votes cast. A well drafted agreement usually provides that it prevails between the parties and obliges them to change the constitution to remove any conflict.

faqs.q: What happens if co-owners fall out and there is no agreement?
faqs.a: The constitution and the Corporations Act decide, and equal owners can find that neither can outvote the other. If the dispute cannot be negotiated, the court can make orders where the company's affairs are conducted oppressively or unfairly against a member, or against the interests of the members as a whole, including that one owner buy the other's shares, and it can order the company to be wound up where that is just and equitable.

faqs.q: How many directors and shareholders does a company need?
faqs.a: A proprietary company needs at least one member and at least one director who ordinarily resides in Australia, and every director must be at least 18. It does not need a company secretary, although it can have one, and it can have no more than 50 shareholders who are not employees. Every director also needs a director identification number.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to set up a company and a shareholder agreement?
faqs.a: Setting up a company is a fixed fee of $660 including GST, and ASIC's registration fee is passed on at cost. A shareholder agreement is from $2,420 including GST for one private company with up to three shareholders who have agreed the commercial terms, and our fees page sets out what each covers.
